\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation: ISR reveals a 99.5\% collapse under exec-only GRPO that PR hides, while SFT localizes the failure to RL optimization (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse observed at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$): tautological proofs receive artificially high ISR (${\geq}0.5$ by construction), creating a positive feedback loop once sampled during rollouts.
The effect is consistent across logic types (Prolog: 0\% non-hacking, 3/3 seeds), model scales (1.7B: novel gaming modes), and training durations (500$\to$1000 steps).
At 500 steps, ISR increases the proportion of genuine proofs relative to random controls ($22.6\%$ vs.\ $7.7\%$; $\text{OR}{=}3.48$, uncorrected); under stricter H8+FN-corrected classification (3-seed subset), OR reduces to $0.61$ (n.s.), and extended training on seed~42 (1000 steps) confirms the genuine window closes ($17\%{\to}2\%$).
ISR is reliable as a diagnostic but unreliable as an optimizer: the same LOO bias that rewards genuine necessity also rewards tautological constructions.

\paragraph{Classifier blind spots and arms-race dynamics.}
H7b (obfuscated tautology), Prolog query-as-fact gaming, and H9 (contradiction injection, 1.7B) demonstrate that text-match classifiers have systematic blind spots exploitable by optimization.
Simple tautology filters would catch H7a but not H7b (triple gaming at $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.83$), query-as-fact ($95/97$ Prolog tautological samples bypassed strict classifier), or H9 (contradictory premises bypass both text-match and functional $n_{\text{necessary}}$ classifiers).
The consistent discovery of novel exploit modes across conditions argues for mandatory functional cross-validation and suggests ISR's vulnerability is not trivially fixable by mode-specific guards.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
$\beta$ controls the \emph{timing} of collapse, not whether it occurs (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); snapshot evaluation overestimates ISR's benefit, and single-seed results can misrepresent a configuration's hacking profile ($\text{CV}{>}1$ across seeds).
Different model capacities converge to different exploit strategies under identical rewards (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}); no safe scale was observed in our single-seed cross-scale evaluation (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).
ISR and similar perturbation-based metrics should serve as post-hoc evaluation tools, not training signals; future work should target gaming-robust reward designs and formal analysis of the stochastic bifurcation dynamics.

\subsection{Cross-Logic Diagnostic Transfer}
\label{sec:crosslogic}

We replicate the FOL pipeline with Prolog/SWI-Prolog (3 seeds, $\beta{=}0.1$).

\paragraph{Hacking taxonomy.}
Across conditions, seeds, and logic types we identify nine structural-degeneration modes (full definitions in Appendix~\ref{app:hacking-modes}).
The numbering (H1, H7, H8) reflects our iterative classification process: intermediate modes H2--H6 were merged into H1 or reclassified as subtypes during analysis (e.g., H2--H5 were variants of conclusion embedding differing only in premise count or formatting, subsumed by H1; H6 was reclassified as a subtype of H7).
The retained modes are:
\textbf{H1} (conclusion embedded among multiple premises),
\textbf{H7} (single-premise conclusion duplication, subtypes H7a standard and H7b obfuscated tautology; targets the ISR signal directly, since removing the sole premise forces $\text{ISR}\geq 0.5$),
\textbf{H8} (premise-subset gaming: each component is LOO-necessary but the premise set is a strict subset of what the problem requires, inflating ISR without faithful reasoning; Appendix~\ref{app:h8}),
\textbf{tautological collapse} (minimal two-component $P{\to}P$ without explicit ISR inflation),
\textbf{repetition collapse} (identical clauses repeated to inflate component count),
\textbf{complexity-without-utility} (elaborate but vacuous premises),
\textbf{contradiction explosion} (contradictory premises trivializing any conclusion via \emph{ex falso}),
\textbf{query-as-fact gaming} (Prolog-specific: emit the NL question as an atom asserted as both fact and query; evades text-match classifiers), and
\textbf{H9: ex falso quodlibet} (contradiction injection: the model generates logically contradictory premises from which any conclusion follows; observed only at 1.7B scale, \S\ref{sec:crossscale}).
Modes are identified by a two-stage procedure: strict normalized text matching (H1/H7) plus functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution (catches modes evading text matching).
We report both classifications in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.
The taxonomy is independently applicable: text matching (H1/H7) requires only string comparison between conclusion and premises, needing no solver or ISR computation; the functional stage uses per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ from any LOO-based analysis, not specifically STA.
Practitioners can apply the taxonomy to any neurosymbolic system where premise--conclusion structure is inspectable.

In interpreting ISR results, we distinguish two failure semantics that share a numerical signature: an exec-only \emph{low} ISR signals \emph{redundancy} (e.g., repeated ground facts in Prolog), whereas an ISR-rewarded \emph{high} ISR signals \emph{metric gaming} (H7-style constructions).
A bare ISR difference therefore does not translate directly into a reasoning-ability difference; the mode breakdown is what licenses such interpretation.
